passages.t: A day of fasting and confession
passages.happening:
‘On the twenty-fourth day of the same month, the Israelites gathered together, fasting and wearing sackcloth, with dust on their heads’ (verse 1).

‘Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from all the foreigners, and they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers’ (verse 2). For a quarter of the day they read from the Book of the Law, and for another quarter they confess and worship (verse 3).

Then the Levites call the people to stand and praise: “Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 8 ended with the joy of the Feast of Tabernacles. Two days after the feast closes, the tone changes to sorrow and confession. This is the mourning that the leaders had told the people to hold back on the holy day.

Fasting, sackcloth, a rough garment of goat or camel hair, and dust on the head were the ordinary signs of mourning and repentance. Standing to confess was a posture of attention before God. The day falls into quarters, three hours or so of reading and three of confession and worship: the pattern of chapter 8, reading and then response.

The separation from foreigners in verse 2 was an act for this occasion. Those of Israelite descent were confessing the sins of their own ancestors, a confession that outsiders could not make on their behalf. To confess the sins of one's fathers alongside one's own was a known form of prayer after the exile. It expressed solidarity with earlier generations rather than blaming them.
passages.later: Daniel prayed in the same way, confessing his own sin and his people's: ‘we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled’ (Daniel 9:5). So did Ezra, who said, ‘From the days of our fathers to this day, our guilt has been great’ (Ezra 9:7).
passages.asks: The people confessed their fathers' sins as well as their own, without blaming the fathers. Ask whether you can own the wrongs of your family, your church or your people honestly, without either excusing them or pointing at others. And ask what it would mean to stand up and praise God on the same day.

passages.t: From creation to the land: what God gave
passages.happening:
The Levites pray, and the prayer retells Israel's story. ‘You alone are the LORD. You created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them. You give life to all things, and the host of heaven worships You’ (verse 6).

God chose Abram, brought him out of Ur, and made a covenant with him to give his descendants the land. ‘You have kept Your promise, because You are righteous’ (verse 8). God saw his people's suffering in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea. He led them with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. He came down at Sinai and gave them good laws and his holy Sabbath. ‘In their hunger You gave them bread from heaven; in their thirst You brought them water from the rock’ (verse 15).

But they became arrogant and stiff-necked. ‘But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them’ (verse 17). Even when they cast an image of a calf and called it their god, God did not abandon them in the wilderness (verses 18-19). ‘For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing’ (verse 21). Then God gave them kingdoms and a good land, ‘So they ate and were filled; they grew fat and delighted in Your great goodness’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the longest prayers in the Bible, and one of the fullest summaries of the Old Testament story told by Israel itself. Behind it stand the books from Genesis to Kings.

The prayer moves in stages, and each stage sets what God did beside what the people did. God creates and chooses; God rescues from Egypt; God guides and gives the law. The people rebel, and God forgives.

It is full of the language of earlier Scripture. Its central confession, that God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, comes from God's own words to Moses after the golden calf. Those words appear again and again in the Old Testament.

The word stiff-necked comes from farm animals that refuse the yoke or the driver's lead. It recurs in the prayer as Israel's characteristic sin. And the word for compassion, rachamim, is related to the Hebrew word for womb. It is the prayer's explanation for why Israel still exists.
passages.later:
God's words to Moses stand behind verse 17: ‘The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness’ (Exodus 34:6).

And the call of Abram: ‘I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess’ (Genesis 15:7).
passages.asks: The prayer remembers God's gifts in detail: bread, water, a pillar of fire, clothes that did not wear out. Ask what gifts of God you would name if you told your own story. And ask where, like Israel in a good land, you have grown comfortable and forgotten the giver.

passages.t: Rebellion, compassion, and slaves in their own land
passages.happening:
‘But they were disobedient and rebelled against You; they flung Your law behind their backs. They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You’ (verse 26). So God handed them over to their enemies, and when they cried out he heard them and gave them deliverers. The pattern repeats again and again. God warned them by his Spirit through the prophets, ‘Yet they would not listen’ (verse 30). ‘But in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them; nor did You forsake them, for You are a gracious and compassionate God’ (verse 31).

Then the prayer turns to the present. It asks God not to treat lightly all the hardship that has come ‘from the days of the kings of Assyria until today’ (verse 32). ‘You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly’ (verse 33).

‘So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness’ (verse 36). The land's harvest goes to the kings set over them because of their sins.

And it ends with a decision: ‘In view of all this, we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests’ (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The setting is the autumn of about 445 BC. Judah was a province of the Persian empire, paying tribute and ruled by the king's officials. Persia had allowed the return and the rebuilding, and Nehemiah himself served the Persian king. Yet the prayer says frankly that their subjection is a result of Israel's sin, and that the harvest of the land goes to foreign kings.

The days of the kings of Assyria reach back to the conquest of the northern kingdom and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. The prayer treats the whole stretch, from then until now, as one long hardship.

The prayer does not excuse itself. It says that God has been just in everything that has happened. And it rests all its hope on his compassion and his covenant, not on the people's record.

The agreement of verse 38 is not the usual word for covenant. It is amanah, a firm commitment, from the same root as amen. The people put it in writing and seal it. Chapter 10 records what they promised.
passages.later:
Stephen, on trial in Jerusalem, retold Israel's story in the same way, with the same charge about the prophets: ‘Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute?’ (Acts 7:52).

The principle of verse 29 comes from the law, ‘for the man who does these things will live by them’ (Leviticus 18:5), and Ezekiel repeats it (Ezekiel 20:11).
passages.hard:
The prayer speaks of God's ordinances ‘by which a man will live if he practices them’ (verse 29). Does this mean that salvation comes by keeping the law?

Verse 29 quotes the principle of Leviticus 18:5, which Ezekiel also repeats. In its setting, the prayer's point is that the law was given for Israel's good, a way of life in the land, and that Israel refused it. Paul later quotes the same principle (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12), setting righteousness based on the law against righteousness based on faith, and that has led to debate about how the two relate.

Interpreters read it in different ways. Many in the Reformation tradition see Leviticus 18:5 as stating a real principle that no sinner can fulfill, which drives people to seek righteousness as a gift. Others argue that in Leviticus the promise of life belonged to a people already rescued by grace from Egypt, so that obedience was the response to salvation and not its cause, and that Paul is setting two ways of reading the law side by side rather than two ways of salvation.

Nehemiah 9 fits either reading. The same prayer that praises the good law rests all of Israel's hope on God's compassion.
passages.asks: The prayer says that God is just and that the people have done wrong, and then it makes a promise. Ask whether you can say both of those things to God without excuses. And ask what promise your own confession should lead to.
